{{Short description|Multiset analogue of matroids}}
{{Refimprove|date=February 2011}}

In mathematics, a '''polymatroid''' is a [[polytope]] associated with a [[submodular function]]. The notion was introduced by [[Jack Edmonds]] in 1970.<ref name="edmonds" /> It is also a generalization of the notion of a [[matroid]].

==Definition==
===Polyhedral definition===
Let <math>E</math> be a finite [[Set (mathematics)|set]] and <math>f: 2^E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}</math> a non-decreasing [[Submodular set function|submodular function]], that is, for each <math> A\subseteq B \subseteq E</math> we have <math> f(A)\leq f(B) </math>, and for each <math> A, B \subseteq E</math> we have <math> f(A)+f(B) \geq f(A\cup B) + f(A\cap B) </math>. We define the '''polymatroid''' associated to <math> f</math> to be the following [[polytope]]:

:<math>P_f= \Big\{\textbf{x}\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^E~\Big|~\sum_{e\in U}\textbf{x}(e)\leq f(U), \forall U\subseteq E\Big\}</math>.

When we allow the entries of <math> \textbf{x} </math> to be negative we denote this polytope by <math>EP_f</math>, and call it the extended polymatroid associated to <math>f</math>.<ref name="schrijver"/>

=== Matroidal definition ===
In matroid theory, polymatroids are defined as the pair consisting of the set and the function as in the above definition. That is, a '''polymatroid''' is a pair <math>(E, f)</math> where <math>E</math> is a [[finite set]] and <math>f:2^E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}</math>, or <math>\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},</math> is a non-decreasing submodular function. If the [[codomain]] is <math>\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},</math> we say that <math>(E,f)</math> is an '''integer polymatroid'''. We call <math>E</math> the '''ground set''' and <math>f</math> the '''rank function''' of the polymatroid. This definition generalizes the definition of a matroid in terms of its rank function. A vector <math>x\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^E</math> is '''independent''' if <math>\sum_{e\in U}x(e)\leq f(U)</math> for all <math>U\subseteq E</math>. Let <math>P</math> denote the set of independent vectors. Then <math>P</math> is the polytope in the previous definition, called the '''independence polytope''' of the polymatroid.<ref name="D Welsh">{{cite book |last1=Welsh |first1=D.J.A. |title=Matroid Theory |date=1976 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=0 12 744050 X |page=338}}</ref>

Under this definition, a matroid is a special case of integer polymatroid. While the rank of an element in a matroid can be either <math>0</math> or <math>1</math>, the rank of an element in a polymatroid can be any nonnegative [[real number]], or nonnegative integer in the case of an integer polymatroid. In this sense, a polymatroid can be considered a multiset analogue of a matroid.

=== Vector definition ===
Let <math>E</math> be a finite [[Set (mathematics)|set]]. If <math> \textbf{u}, \textbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^E</math> then we denote by <math>|\textbf{u}|</math> the sum of the entries of <math>\textbf{u}</math>, and write <math> \textbf{u} \leq \textbf{v}</math> whenever <math> \textbf{v}(i)-\textbf{u}(i)\geq 0</math> for every <math>i \in E</math> (notice that this gives a [[Partially ordered set|partial order]] to <math>\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^E</math>). A '''polymatroid''' on the ground set <math>E</math> is a nonempty [[Compact (mathematics)|compact]] subset <math>P</math>, the set of independent vectors, of <math> \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^E</math> such that:
# If <math> \textbf{v} \in P</math>, then <math> \textbf{u} \in P</math> for every <math> \textbf{u}\leq \textbf{v}.</math>
# If <math> \textbf{u},\textbf{v} \in P</math> with <math> |\textbf{v}|> |\textbf{u}|</math>, then there is a vector <math>\textbf{w}\in P</math> such that <math> \textbf{u}<\textbf{w}\leq (\max\{\textbf{u}(1),\textbf{v}(1)\},\dots,\max\{\textbf{u}({|E|}),\textbf{v}({|E|})\}).</math>

This definition is equivalent to the one described before,<ref name="Herzog"/> where <math> f</math> is the function defined by 
:<math> f(A) = \max\Big\{\sum_{i\in A} \textbf{v}(i)~\Big|~ \textbf{v} \in P\Big\}</math> for every <math> A\subseteq E</math>.

The second property may be simplified to 
:If <math> \textbf{u},\textbf{v} \in P</math> with <math> |\textbf{v}|> |\textbf{u}|</math>, then <math>(\max\{\textbf{u}(1),\textbf{v}(1)\},\dots,\max\{\textbf{u}({|E|}),\textbf{v}({|E|})\})\in P.</math>
Then compactness is implied if <math>P</math> is assumed to be bounded.

==Discrete polymatroids ==
A '''discrete polymatroid''' or '''integral polymatroid''' is a polymatroid for which the codomain of <math>f</math> is <math>\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}</math>, so the vectors are in <math> \mathbb{Z}^E_{\geq 0}</math> instead of <math> \mathbb{R}^E_{\geq 0}</math>. Discrete polymatroids can be understood by focusing on the [[lattice points]] of a polymatroid, and are of great interest because of their relationship to [[Monomial ideal|monomial ideals]].

Discrete polymatroids are related to matroids.
Given a positive integer <math>k</math>, a discrete polymatroid <math>(E,f)</math> (using the matroidal definition) is a '''<math>k</math>-polymatroid''' if <math> f(e) \leq k </math> for all <math> e \in E </math>. Thus, a <math>1</math>-polymatroid is a matroid.
Also, for any discrete polymatroid <math>(E, f)</math>, there is a matroid whose independent sets are the sets <math>A \subseteq E</math> such that <math>f(U) \ge |U|</math> for all <math>U \subseteq A</math>.<ref name="oxley">{{cite book
 |last=Oxley |first=James  |author-link=James Oxley
 |year=1992
 |title=Matroid Theory
 |publisher=Oxford University Press
 |location=Oxford, UK
 |isbn=978-0-19-853563-8
 |mr=1207587 |zbl=0784.05002
}}</ref>

==Relation to generalized permutahedra==
A '''generalized permutahedron''' (alternative spelling: permutohedron) is a [[polytope]] whose [[normal fan]] is a coarsening of the '''braid fan''', defined by the hyperplanes <math>x_j = x_k</math> in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>; note that the braid fan is the normal fan of the standard [[permutahedron]]. Thus the geometry of generalized permutahedra is intimately connected to the combinatorics of the [[symmetric group]].

Alternatively, a generalized permutahedron can be characterized as a polytope obtained by parallel translations of the facets of the standard [[permutahedron]].<ref>{{citation|last=Postnikov|first=Alexander|arxiv=math.CO/0507163|doi=10.1093/imrn/rnn153|issue=6|journal=International Mathematics Research Notices|mr=2487491|pages=1026–1106|title=Permutohedra, associahedra, and beyond|year=2009|volume=2009 }}
</ref>
Thus <math>P</math> is a generalized permutahedron precisely if

<math display=block>
P = \left\{
x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \, 
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = z_{[n]}, \ \sum_{i \in S} x_i \ge z_S
\, \text{ for all nonempty } \,
S \subseteq [n]
\right\}
</math>

for some submodular function <math>z: 2^{[n]} \to \mathbb{R}</math>.

The [[0/1-polytope]]s among generalized permutahedra are precisely the [[matroid polytope]]s.

==Properties==
<math>P_f</math> is nonempty [[if and only if]] <math>f\geq 0</math> and that <math>EP_f</math> is nonempty if and only if <math>f(\emptyset)\geq 0</math>.

Given any extended polymatroid <math>EP</math> there is a unique submodular function <math>f</math> such that <math>f(\emptyset)=0</math> and <math>EP_f=EP</math>.

==Contrapolymatroids==
For a [[supermodular]] ''f'' one analogously may define the '''contrapolymatroid'''
:<math>\Big\{w \in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^E~\Big|~\forall S \subseteq E, \sum_{e\in S}w(e)\ge f(S)\Big\}</math>.
This analogously generalizes the dominant of the [[spanning set#Matroids|spanning set]] [[polytope]] of matroids.
